reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is framed as a tutorial on sourcing products, building a brand, launching products, and selling through online marketplaces. The displayed profit calculation and Rs 2,73,000 monthly projection are presented as instructional figures, without establishing that the result occurred or was guaranteed. The advice about seeking purchases and reviews from relatives and offering discounted products for reviews is a review-generation tactic, but the available video evidence does not establish actual reviews, undisclosed compensation, or transaction outcomes.

opening.argument: The video links an apparently easy income outcome to concrete financial participation. It says viewers will learn how someone earns 1 lakh per month and how they can do the same, then directs them to buy low-cost goods, send them to Amazon FBA, and resell them. The proposed action is therefore not merely educational: viewers are encouraged to purchase inventory and enter a marketplace workflow in pursuit of a highly specific monthly return. The presentation further states that carrying out the model on two websites will produce Rs 2,73,000 per month. That combination of a strong income expectation and a simple operational path makes this function as an income solicitation, even if the figures are described through examples.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the material a tutorial does not remove the solicitation. The tutorial repeatedly connects the viewer's purchases and resale activity to projected income, while the reference-side description treats the central numerical promise as merely hypothetical. But the video presents a specific monthly profit and a concrete path to pursue it. Its review advice also shows that success depends on manufacturing early positive signals, not simply explaining ordinary commerce.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted income statements do not establish a guaranteed or easy payout. The video describes a resale model requiring inventory, marketplace sales, supplier selection, branding, advertising, and product ranking. Its numerical example is a projection tied to stated assumptions, not proof that viewers will receive money. The review advice may be questionable, but it still does not show that the speaker collected funds, delivered a promised return, or operated a fraudulent payment flow.

citations.quote: WE HAVE SHOWN YOU HOW YOU CAN PURCHASE PRODUCTS FROM ALIBABA.COM AND HOW YOU CAN YOU CAN SELL IT ON AMAZON OR ANY OTHER WEBSITES
You have chosen your product and did its branding Now finally comes how you will bring your product back to Amazon
If you do this on 2 websites, your monthly profit will be Rs 2,73,000.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: unusually large projected returns, an external free-download link, and instructions to create favorable reviews so products rank and sell. The video promotes a model in which viewers buy goods cheaply, resell them at much higher prices, and are told that two websites can yield Rs 2,73,000 monthly. It also directs viewers to obtain five-star ratings from relatives and to offer products at very low prices in exchange for reviews. Those features make the promised income look dependent on engineered social proof and optimistic margins rather than demonstrated demand. The combination is materially more concerning than a neutral explanation of online retail.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference-side opening minimizes the strongest warning signs by saying the evidence does not establish actual reviews or transactions. Actual completion is not required to identify a deceptive pitch: the video itself supplies the requested review manipulation and pairs it with a high profit projection. The external free-download link and repeated calls to subscribe and contact the channel also make the material promotional, not a detached demonstration.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are risk indicators, not proof of a scam. The link is presented as a free audiobook download, but the evidence does not show a payment, credential request, or harmful outcome. Likewise, the review instruction is visible, yet no actual review, transaction, or concealed compensation is established. The profit figure is explicitly part of a resale calculation, and a concerning marketing tactic does not convert ordinary product sourcing into a fraudulent income scheme.

opening.argument: Although the video adopts the format of education, its overall role is promotional. It presents a complete business blueprint, emphasizes freedom and high monthly profit, instructs viewers how to launch and rank products, and ends by directing them to subscribe and contact the channel. The content therefore steers viewers toward participation in a purportedly accessible income opportunity. The promotional framing is reinforced by the direct invitation to buy and resell products through the described supply chain and by the promise that the model can provide both substantial money and free time. This is not simply analysis of e-commerce; it is a pitch for viewers to act on the model.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The label of tutorial is not decisive when the content ends with subscription and contact instructions and repeatedly sells the lifestyle outcome. The reference-side opening focuses on whether the profit calculation was proven, but promotion can be misleading through aspirational framing even without a documented completed transaction. Here, the model is presented as a complete blueprint and tied to freedom, high income, and viewer participation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotional presentation does not itself prove fraudulent income solicitation. The calls to subscribe and contact the channel are ordinary audience-building language, while the central material explains sourcing, fulfillment, branding, and marketplace sales. The phrase “blueprint” describes the tutorial's scope, not a guaranteed payout. The evidence also does not show that viewers were asked to pay the channel, transfer funds, or receive a promised return.
